claims.text: Adding silicon to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The proposed intervention is the addition of 1–3 atomic percent silicon.
The hypothesis is intended to apply during exposure to air or another oxidizing atmosphere at 1200°C for 100 hours.
Silicon addition will produce a continuous silicon oxide layer on the alloy surface.
The silicon oxide layer will be adherent to the alloy surface.
The surface silicon oxide will be SiO2.
Silicon in the alloy preferentially oxidizes at high temperature.
The resulting SiO2 layer is dense and stable under the specified conditions.
The SiO2 layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion prevents further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
The silicon-modified alloy will have significantly lower oxidation-associated mass gain than the untreated alloy after exposure under the specified conditions.
The untreated alloy is expected to have higher mass gain than the silicon-modified alloy.
The untreated alloy may form oxides that are less protective than the proposed SiO2 layer.
The proposed benefit requires sufficient silicon solubility in the RHEA.
The proposed benefit requires conditions under which SiO2 remains stable and is not reduced by alloying elements or the environment.
The effectiveness of silicon addition may depend on the specific RHEA composition and interactions with other alloying elements.
Failure to reduce mass gain or failure to form a continuous protective SiO2 layer relative to the untreated control is proposed as a falsifying result.
